issue_context.title: max requests on a socket
issue_context.body:
## 🚀 Feature Proposal

In keep-alive response header, there is a posibility to define the timeout and max requests for the connection
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Keep-Alive
 
I would like propose the functionality on the server, that will count requests per socket and send "connection: closed" header and actually close the connection when it reached the maximum value

## Motivation

Currently as fast as I can understand, nothing can force the connection on the server to be closed, for example both 
"connectionTimeout" and "keepAliveTimeout" define the time of inactivity, for the socket to be closed, but if the socket is always active, or the client ignores this header, server will not send the "connection: close" header and close the connection
comments: My understanding is that those two config options should be enough and remove idle connections. Can you please make a code example on why they are not enough?

@mcollina Thanks, but the problem is that I do not want to handle idle connection, I want to handle active connections, I want to force rebalancing by closing active connections
as far as I understood this is exactly what "max" property on "keep-alive" header is doing, defining max requests per connection

The keep-alive header is managed by Node.js core, not Fastify. It should be managed there (similarly to the timeout property).

I'm not exactly sure how this property would work and/if the load balancers will interpret it

It seems it could live in a plugin, why would you like to add it to Fastify proper?

I'm not really sure what's the goal of this feature, why would you want to recycle the connection?

> I'm not really sure what's the goal of this feature, why would you want to recycle the connection?

When we have a spike of high traffic, we see that autoscaling does not help since there are already opened connections to existing pods that never closed to be assigned to new scaled pods

> It seems it could live in a plugin, why would you like to add it to Fastify proper?

I don't know if its a good practice for a plugin to destroy(!) sockets that are managed by fastify

It's ok, there are no side effects.

Anyhow, I'm not sure this would lead to the results you want.
Thanks, closing
This is better handled at the reverse proxy by setting appropriate headers and configuration there. Your application should not have to worry about load balancing logic.

@jsumners this is internal traffic inside k8s cluster, when some pods are scaled up, other pods does not reconnect to new ones, it can be handled by some sidecar like LinkerD or Istio but they have other issue and overhead

this are the results BTW 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/57314588/130417967-3d2eec5f-756d-4e3e-ad00-ec232c913a0e.png)


CPU distribution across pods before/after

Just curious, these are the results when having a finite number of sockets active on code?
Looks pretty stable and nice being honest, but I'm wondering if it really needs to be handled by the service itself

This seems something we might want to add in Node.js, as it's the one managing the keep-alive logic.

In the meanwhile, would you like to add that logic to a fastify plugin?

Really good results @artur-ma!
@ronag wdyt? Should we add "maxRequestPerConnection" or analog to HTTP/1.1 keep-alive?
I'm good with `maxRequestPerConnection` if it is included in the keep-alive hint as `max`. The default should be Infinite. IMO.
@artur-ma would you like to open an issue (or even a PR) on Node.js core?
@mcollina Does it need a plugin now? I think it should be resolved by https://github.com/nodejs/node/commit/4e8f11dee3b7dcea7472058f4182ddd36b86c781 in core.
it will need a PR against Fastify once that is released
And `16.10.0` is released with this: https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v16.10.0/

Hi! I saw the original motivation for this change being to force rebalancing. As far as I can tell, it fulfills a similar function to an HTTP/2 ALTSVC frame (or an Alt-Svc header for both HTTP/1.1 and 2) - telling clients they should possibly go to another server, although the technical implementation of this transition is completely different. The two are not related in any way, right? The new option doesn't impact HTTP/2?

Just occurred to me that, with the overarching goal being service load balancing, Fastify might one day have an option (or a plugin?) to do that, where the appropriate headers are preferred, but if the client doesn't switch servers soon (because e.g. it ignores the hint), it gets disconnected after several more requests. I'd welcome your thoughts on this.
